When your Wolf 3D based game ends up being worse to control than Super 3-D Noah's Ark, you did badly.

Blake Stone: Aliens of Gold, developed by JAM Productions and published by Apogee Entertainment, is a fascinating relic from the formative years of the first-person shooter genre, arriving at a time when developers were still experimenting with what the format could become. Set in a futuristic world where a rogue scientist is engineering a monstrous army, the game casts players as Blake Stone, a suave secret agent tasked with infiltrating high-tech facilities and stopping a looming global threat. While the premise is pulpy and straightforward, it provides a fitting backdrop for a game that is more concerned with mechanical iteration than narrative complexity, using its science fiction setting to distinguish itself from the war-themed shooters that inspired it.

At its core, the gameplay builds upon the framework established by earlier genre pioneers, particularly the corridor-based structure and fast-paced shooting of early 90s titles. Movement is quick and direct, gunplay is immediate, and levels are designed as interconnected mazes filled with locked doors, hidden passages, and roaming enemies. However, what sets Blake Stone apart is its effort to expand on that formula in subtle but meaningful ways. The addition of a persistent automap reduces some of the frustration associated with navigating complex layouts, while the inclusion of neutral characters—informants who can provide hints or resources—adds an unexpected layer of interaction. These elements may seem modest by modern standards, but at the time they represented a clear attempt to make the world feel more responsive and less purely hostile.

The game’s structure is notably ambitious for its era, offering multiple episodes composed of several floors each, all of which can be revisited. This design encourages exploration and rewards thoroughness, as players can return to earlier areas to uncover secrets or gather missed supplies. It also creates a sense of continuity within each episode, making the facilities feel more like cohesive spaces rather than isolated levels. However, this approach comes with trade-offs. The reliance on maze-like layouts and repeated visual motifs can lead to disorientation, especially in later stages where complexity increases. Without strong visual landmarks, it becomes easy to lose track of objectives, turning exploration into trial-and-error navigation.

Combat is straightforward but effective, built around a small arsenal of progressively more powerful weapons and a variety of enemies that range from armed guards to grotesque mutants and alien creatures. While enemy behavior is relatively simple, the game compensates through encounter design, often surprising players with ambushes or unexpected enemy placements. Resource management also plays a role, as ammunition and health are limited enough to require careful consideration without becoming overly restrictive. The overall result is a gameplay loop that remains engaging, even if it lacks the depth and dynamism seen in later entries in the genre.

Visually, the game represents an incremental step forward from its predecessors. The addition of textured floors and ceilings gives environments a greater sense of depth, and the bright, almost exaggerated color palette helps reinforce its science fiction identity. Despite these improvements, the limitations of the underlying technology are still apparent. Environments can feel repetitive, with similar corridors and rooms appearing frequently, which contributes to the sense of monotony over extended play sessions. The presentation is functional and occasionally charming, but it struggles to maintain visual variety across the game’s considerable length.

One of the most interesting aspects of Blake Stone: Aliens of Gold is its place in gaming history. Released just before the arrival of a genre-defining title that would dramatically shift expectations for first-person shooters, it was quickly overshadowed despite its innovations. In retrospect, it feels like a bridge between two eras—a game that takes meaningful steps forward while still being firmly rooted in older design philosophies. Its contributions, while often overlooked, hint at ideas that would become standard in later games, making it more significant than its reputation might suggest.

From a modern standpoint, the game can feel dated in several respects. Its repetitive environments, simplistic enemy AI, and occasionally confusing level design may test the patience of players accustomed to more refined experiences. Yet there is an undeniable appeal in its straightforward design and earnest attempts to evolve the genre. For those with an interest in retro gaming or the history of first-person shooters, it offers valuable insight into how the genre developed during a period of rapid experimentation and change.

In the end, Blake Stone: Aliens of Gold is not a timeless masterpiece, but it is a meaningful and enjoyable piece of FPS history. It delivers a solid and occasionally inventive take on early shooter mechanics, even if it is ultimately eclipsed by more influential titles released around the same time. Its charm lies in its ambition and its willingness to push beyond established boundaries, making it a worthwhile experience for players willing to look past its age and appreciate its role in shaping what came next.

[h1]Blake Stone: Aliens of Gold. O elo perdido entre Wolfenstein e Doom[/h1]

[b]“Antes de arrancar demônios do inferno, arrancamos mutantes de laboratórios mal iluminados.”[/b]

[h2]1. A promessa de um novo herói dos anos 90[/h2]

Quando Blake Stone: Aliens of Gold chegou em 1993, a Apogee tentou apresentar ao mundo um novo ícone dos FPS, Blake Stone era um agente do British Intelligence enfrentando o maluco Dr. Pyrus Goldfire, um cientista que transformava pessoas em mutantes grotescos para construir um exército próprio, o jogo apostava em ficção científica pulsante, cheia de lasers, robôs, criaturas deformadas e instalações futuristas, quase como se um quadrinho pulp dos anos 80 tivesse virado um videogame.

Havia ambição, havia energia e havia uma tentativa sincera de ir muito além da fórmula de Wolfenstein 3D, a ideia central era simples, mas charmosa, explorar bases científicas, sobreviver a mutações bizarras e impedir que Goldfire espalhasse sua “visão dourada” pelo universo.

[b]“Se Wolfenstein era aço e concreto, Blake Stone era neon, mutações e paranóia científica.”[/b]

[h2]2. A evolução de Wolfenstein presa no passado[/h2]

Mesmo usando o motor de Wolfenstein 3D, Blake Stone tentava empurrar tudo ao limite, ele adicionou mapas mais variados, painéis tecnológicos, salas laboratoriais, ambientes que pareciam realmente funcionais, e até NPCs aliados. algo raríssimo em FPS da época, os inimigos eram mais diversificados, indo além de soldados genéricos e trazendo monstros verdadeiramente memoráveis, mas a engine limitava tudo, os corredores eram planos, a movimentação era rígida, a variedade visual tentava mascarar a repetição estrutural, o jogo queria ser moderno, mas sua fundação pertencia ao passado, mesmo assim, as intenções eram claras, dar mais vida e mais identidade ao mundo, Blake Stone não era só um tiro em corredor, era um tiro em corredor, laboratório, sala de teste, câmara de experimento e área de pesquisa.

[b]“Blake Stone queria correr… mas o motor Wolf3D só deixava ele caminhar.”[/b]

[h2]3. O brilho da atmosfera sci-fi e seus monstros[/h2]

Onde Blake Stone se destaca é na personalidade visual, os mutantes de Goldfire têm designs marcantes, a paleta de cores parece saída de uma HQ psicodélica e os laboratórios transmitem a sensação de um mundo vivo e funcional, cada corredor metálico, cada sala repleta de painéis piscando e cada câmara com experimentos grotescos reforçam o charme retrofuturista do jogo.

É um sci-fi colorido, exagerado, quase caricatural e exatamente por isso é tão divertido, mesmo limitado, o jogo se esforça para parecer maior do que realmente é.

[h2]4. Jogabilidade. ambição que tropeça em suas próprias pernas[/h2]

O ponto mais controverso do jogo é sua jogabilidade, há boas ideias, os NPCs inocentes que você pode poupar, sistemas de segurança que podem ser desligados, armas futuristas, exploração recompensadora, mas o ritmo é lento, os inimigos são resistentes demais, os mapas são grandes ao ponto de parecerem arrastados e a repetição estrutural, típica da engine, pesa após algumas horas.

O jogo tinha ambições de modernidade, mais do que a plataforma podia entregar, ele queria oferecer liberdade, narrativa contextual e variedade… mas sempre esbarrava no “pavimento plano” do motor Wolfenstein, ainda assim, a experiência carrega charme, por trás de seus limites, há um jogo tentando honestamente fazer mais do que podia, Wolfenstein como ponto de partida, mas Doom como ponto de queda.

Se compararmos apenas a Wolfenstein 3D, Blake Stone é uma evolução gigantesca, mais conteúdo, mais personalidade, mais mecânicas, mais variedade, ele é praticamente Wolfenstein com esteroides científicos, mas o problema de Blake Stone não foi ser melhor ou pior que Wolfenstein, o problema foi o calendário, Doom lançou apenas seis semanas depois e quando Doom explodiu com sua iluminação dinâmica, mapas verticais, monstros avançados e velocidade alucinante, Blake Stone instantaneamente pareceu velho, ele não perdeu por falhar, perdeu porque Doom inaugurou uma nova era no exato momento errado.

[b]“Blake Stone não foi derrotado pelo que fez… e sim pelo que Doom fez.”[/b]

[h2]5. Da recepção morna ao status cult[/h2]

O jogo vendeu decentemente, mas nunca empolgou o suficiente para competir, acrítica disse: “é bom, mas já nasceu datado”, os jogadores migraram rapidamente para Doom, e Blake Stone caiu no esquecimento, mas o tempo foi gentil, com a onda retrô dos anos 2000 e 2010, fãs de FPS antigos revisitaram o game e perceberam seu valor, humor bizarro, estética única, design exagerado, trilha curiosa, e aquele charme “tecnológico de laboratório dos anos 90” que não existe mais.

[b]Hoje, ele é cult.
Hoje, ele vive na memória dos fãs do gênero.
Hoje, ele é o último suspiro da era Wolfenstein antes da era Doom.[/b]

[h2]6. Conclusão. Um herói esmagado pela história, mas não apagado[/h2]

Blake Stone: Aliens of Gold é um jogo que importa não pelo que mudou, mas pelo que tentou ser, ele marca o fim de uma era, a era dos corredores planos, dos sprites simples, dos mapas quadrados, e o início de outra, que ele não pôde acompanhar, é um retrofuturismo involuntário, uma ficção científica colorida presa no corpo de um motor antiquado, uma tentativa sincera de evolução que foi atropelada por uma revolução, mas, visto hoje, é exatamente isso que o torna especial.

[b]“Blake Stone não venceu sua época, mas resistiu a ela, e hoje brilha como ouro nostálgico.”[/b]

id softwareが開発しジャンルの方向性を決定付けたFPS『Wolfenstein 3D』をベースに、レトロフューチャーなSFへと拡張されたFPS。
エレベーターやバリア、壁スイッチ、中立NPCとの会話、自販機と金銭システムなどなど小手先のギミックを多く取り入れている反面、根本的な部分(グラフィックやマップ構造など)はWolfenstein 3Dから抜け出せておらず、チープな見た目となっている。

開発元はJAM Productionで、この会社はかつてのid softwareメンバーがゲーム雑誌「Softdisk」のふろくゲーム制作をやめて独立した後、欠員を補充しようとSoftdisk社が雇った新たなメンバーがまたもや独立する形で立ち上げられている。
要するに彼らは[b]一躍ヒットメーカーとなったid softwareに憧れて追従しようとした人々[/b]なのだが、当のid softwareは無慈悲にも本作と同じ1993年末に超名作『DOOM』を発売してしまい、前作『Wolfenstein 3D』を基にしているBlake stoneは発売からわずか7日後に時代遅れに。
結局その後もアメリカンドリームは掴めないまま、続編『Blake Stone: Planet Strike』と合わせて2作品を出しただけで倒産してしまった。


ゲーム自体は元となるWolfesntein 3Dに酷似しているため、アローキー+Ctrl+Space+Altの操作性に馴染みがあればとっつきやすい内容。やることも概ね同じで、鍵を集めつつゴールを目指していく。やたら多いミッション数と代わり映えのしないマップに途中から飽きてくるが、ここらへんは価値観の違いもあるだろうか。


別に極端な欠点もなく時代相応の出来ではあるものの、『DOOM』に勝てなかった原因は数多く見つかる悲しいFPS。当時はこんなんが沢山生えてきてる時代の真っただ中だったわけで、そういう埋もれた歴史を掘り返して「もったいないなぁ…」と思いたい時はこのゲームを遊んでみよう。

なお、同じくWolf3Dエンジンの改良版を使用してたら『DOOM』が出てきて酷い目に遭った『Rise of the triad』シリーズとの抱き合わせ4本パックである[u]『The Apogee Throwback Pack』[/u]もSteamで販売されており、こちらを買うことでも本作を触ることができる。単品で買うよりもお買い得なので(どちらにせよジュース以下のはした金だが)、とりあえず適当に触りたいだけならそっちを買うほうが良いかもしれない。

With this being my first time playing Blake Stone, I enjoyed it overall. The experience back at the time of release probably would have been more astonishing, but Doom was still quite a bit better than this.

The story being rather simple, Blake Stone is an agent that is tasked with stopping Dr. Goldfire from controlling the world with his soldiers and monsters. With levels being designed very much like Wolfenstein 3D, the player must blast through about 60 levels to stop Goldfire's plans. If you have played Wolf 3D, this sounds daunting, but I feel the levels and game play of Blake Stone are better. There are about 30 different enemy types, 5 weapons, more detailed textures, and much more developed levels. While Wolfenstein 3D can be fun, it is very tiresome as it can get stale quickly and the levels feel too maze-like with too few variation in graphics or landmarks. Blake Stone still has maze levels, most rooms aren't simple boxes most times, and have plants or tables or other environmental uniqueness to help one remember where a room is. It isn't as good as Doom's map, but it is still more helpful than not having one.

There are quite a few features that stand apart from Wolfenstein 3D, Doom, Heretic, or Quake. Blake Stone showcases some natural textures for natural levels, but most are space station and military or research facilities. There are vending machines around levels that can give you some health for a ration. The 5th weapon is an explosive type, unfortunately all weapons share the same ammo pool like Wolf 3D. Secret push walls, keys, and fast-paced shooting similar to other games of the time.

The music and sound design are great (Apogee were pretty strong in this area). Very distinct sounds for each enemy and good feedback for everything happening in the game.

No bugs found when playing through, but quite a few issues to note. I would highly recommend using a source port to make the experience more enjoyable (more options and settings to mess with) Turning the heartbeat sound and the annoying game over scenes are reason enough to download it. Aside from that, it will take some time to get use to. Especially in 1x1 hallways where you are as wide as the corridors. If you are a retro shooter fan or are looking for an experience similar to Wolfenstein 3D, this game is for you.

I honestly can't believe someone made Blake Stone work on a modern PC. I was obsessed with this game as a kid. Today, not so much. After playing it for a little bit, I have to admit it does not stand the test of time. What a weird jank-fest of early 3D FPS. REVIEW #79
Blake Stone: Aliens of Gold
-------

I've been playing Blake Stone (or at least the demo version) for at least 30 years at this point, and I really enjoyed it as a teen, so I have a lot of potent, pleasantly nostalgic feelings attached to this game. Since I've been on an old-school FPS kick lately, I figured that I'd jump into the full version and give the whole thing a go with the assumption that I'd undoubtedly enjoy my pixelated trip down memory lane. Yeah... it didn't quite happen like that.

For those who are unfamiliar with the short-lived Blake Stone franchise, this first entry (out of 2) is a 90s-era first-person shooter that builds off of Wolfenstein 3D's tech. This means that the game doesn't have any height variance at all, and the player moves around with classic "tank" controls. That's not necessarily a bad thing, as other enjoyable games from Blake Stone's era have these limitations. Textures are bright and colorful (albeit a bit repetitive at times) and some of the graphics feature interesting details, like red alarm lights on the ceiling that only flash after you've fired a shot from a non-silent weapon. BS:AOG also features one of the best automaps that I've seen in a classic game, going so far as to show your stats for that level (like percentages of enemies defeated and allies still living.)

Combat certainly can have its satisfying moments, although the auto aim is a little wonky and can target friendly characters at times, even when they're farther away from center than an enemy. 4 of the 5 available weapons share the same ammo pool, but unlike preceding games, each weapons feels like it has a proper use or time and place to be properly utilized. Learning how and when to run and strafe is key to facing more powerful enemies at higher difficulty levels. However, the tougher difficulties can make BS:AOG start to feel like a rage game, especially at an episode's beginning moments, when you don't have stronger weaponry and have to battle tougher foes to get it.

Additionally, exploration is a bit dull. Again, repetitive textures can make areas feel a bit "same-y", and hunting for treasure can deteriorate into holding the use key down while you slide your face against each wall until an arbitrary secret wall  moves. Collecting treasure increases your score and can earn you extra lives, but since there's a quick-save feature, both life and score counters mean next to nothing during game play.

Thus far, I admit that all of the negatives for this game would be tolerable. To be fair, it has its share of good elements, as BS:AOG has a sense of style that's strangely pleasing, and Bobby Prince did a pretty good job making a catchy selection of background tunes that occasionally caused me to hum along as I blasted foes.

What really killed any chance of me recommending this game is the existence of bugs, specifically occasional invisible walls. In one case, such a bug blocked me from advancing down a necessary path to complete the level. Chances are, I could've started over (as all of my save points had this issue) or even used a source port like BSTONE to avoid a reoccurrence, but neither actions should be necessary for a purchased game, regardless of its price (currently $2 USD). I understand that it's an old game that's no longer supported or updated, but that just makes it worse, as the aforementioned bug encounter totally ended the fun that I was having, and I know that there's almost no chance that a game sold in such a fashion that it still launches in DosBOX will ever have an official fix.

Again, there are probably workarounds to these issues, and some people may want to work through the negatives that I've discussed here, but I think that there's enough here to weigh against Blake Stone: Aliens of Gold that I can't confidently recommend it for purchase unless someone REALLY wants a fairly flawed retro-shooter experience with decent music.

W3D & Doom started the whole FPS craze.

FPP - First Person Perspective
FPS - First Person Shooter
Doom clone - term that was used from '92 to '96 (release of Quake) that means the same as FPS, just doom was so groundbreaking that every other fps game was compared to it.

All of FPS are FPP, but not all FPP are FPS.The alternative being third-person perspective -- or TPP -- which, technically speaking, should include any game where you're looking at the character you're controlling from the outside, but which, in practice, is usually used to describe games with an over-the-shoulder "follow cam" (as opposed to "isometric", top-down, side-view, and probably others).

The FPS term wasn't widely used before release of Quake, before that they were all called "Doom Clones" or FPP. Doom was actually the first game that brought recognition to the FPS genre as something distinct (even though there are games that fit FPS description and predate doom about 19 years, Id themselves released at least 3 FPS games before doom - Hovertank 3D, Catacomb 3-D and Wolfenstein 3D)

So if you want to be specific use FPS, if for example you want to talk about System Shock or Deus Ex use FPP as they're mix of FPS and RPG. And all games that came after doom and before quake can be called doom clones (heretic, hexen, duke nukem 3d, shadow warrior e.t.c.)

There's also a subgenre of FPP that contains vehicular combat (i.e. descent series) that some consider to be FPS and some do not so in this case it's safer to use FPP.

Blake stone is a game that was sadly overlooked in it's time. The swan song of the Wolfenstein 3D engine, it was doomed to obscurity as soon as the game changer known as doom released. fortunately for those of us who choose to go back and judge these games on their own merits instead of technological advancements, it's just so happens to be a wonderful upgrade to ID's maze-like nazi slaughterfest. 

In the game you play as the titular Sci-fi secret agent flash-gordon-meets-james-bond  extraordinaire Blake Stone, who happens to have some upgrades over his predecessor BJ Blascowitz. the base game has six episodes featuring eleven levels each, two of which are secret, for a grand total of 66 levels. during an episode you can travel back and forth between levels you've previously cleared. I used this feature more than once to go back and resupply on health and ammo and it was a very welcome addition to the formula. 

the weapon variety is now slightly enhanced. The first four weapons are merely laser versions of a standard arsenal, though the last two are new additions, one being a super-chaingun and the other being a rocket launcher by any other name. small additions, though welcome ones. 

the enemy variety is now off the charts. aliens, soldiers, turrets, mutants, and dozens of variants therein, the visual variety adds a lot to the atmosphere and immersion of the setting. unfortunately gameplay wise it still boils down to either a hitscanner or a projectile enemy, with some melee only enemies thrown in for good measure. it does do better than wolfenstein in that department as well, though, it doesn't save projectile enemies solely for boss fights and uses them freely amongst the roster. 

finally, the environments are very detailed and filled out for a game of this style. multiple textures and object decorations are filled to the brim with small details that make wolf3D's brick walls feel amateurish in comparison. 

it's a shame that this game released when it did, if it hadn't gotten superseded by doom so fast Blake would probably another in the long like of notable PC protagonists to come fro the 90's. this is truly worthy of it's status as a forgotten classic.

Blake Stone: Aliens of Gold is another one of those games that I played when I was a little 5 year old kid on my friends' computer, along with Wolfenstein 3D and Doom. Regardless of being absolutely useless at it at the time due to not understanding the requirements, something about the title stuck with me through the years, and after sitting in my Steam library unplayed for a not insignificant amount of time, I finally decided to give it a try.

With the BStone source port, this game is transformed into a very easily playable and entertaining old school FPS arcade experience. One thing that I appreciate about Blake Stone in comparison to Wolfenstein 3D is the inclusion of an automap, which makes the experience a lot less cumbersome.

In spite of extremely dated graphics (this game will be 30 years old next year), I have found it to be quite immersive with the colourful palate, allied NPCs and rather varied enemy selection (for the time of release). 

The soundtrack, which was created by Bobby Prince of ID Software fame, is a nice addition, and manages to add to the action in spite of the shortness and limited amount of looping tracks.

Overall, Blake Stone: Aliens of Gold is a product of it's time which, thanks to a great and easy to install source port, can still be quite an entertaining experience in the modern day. If you are hankering for a retro FPS experience other than the usual Dooms, Quakes and Heretics, don't hesitate to give Blake Stone a try.

(Don't let my low playtime here on Steam fool you. I played the  'BStone' sourceport version many times before in the past and just recently bought the game on Steam. Now onto the review....)
The Blake Stone games are some really underrated 'hidden gems' of the retro FPS genre, in my opinion. It takes the Wolf3D engine and just dials everything up to 11, making Wolfenstein3D look like an extremely mediocre and boring game in comparison. I don't even mean any disrespect to Wolf3D at all. Blake Stone is really just that good. Despite using the Wolf3D engine, the graphics are a bit better I think. The detail on textures and sprites is a bit superior to Wolf3D. 
You also have more weapons available to you in Blake Stone. And a few more on top of that in the second Blake Stone game. And all the weapons are more interesting and fun to use than the Wolf3D weapons, I think (with the exception of the God-like Wolf3D chaingun, maybe). In addition to a larger variety of weapons that are more interesting to use, Blake Stone games also have a larger variety of enemies than Wolf3D. And like the difference between Wolf3D and Blake Stone weapons, I think the enemy sprites in Blake Stone are a bit more interesting in general.
The map design is more interesting and engaging to navigate and explore, compared to Wolfenstein 3D. The map design and geometry is still very restrictive, just as it is in Wolf3D, but the developers really did the best anyone could do with the Wolf3D engine I think. 
There's also more game mechanics in Blake Stone games, such as collecting in-game currency tokens to use in vending machines you find scattered throughout maps. These vending machines dispense health if needed. Instead of gold and silver keys like Wolf3D, there's the familiar Doom-styled colored keycards. 
The more I played this game, the more impressed I was. The more surprised I was that all of this was in the Wolf3D engine still. Despite the unmistakable Wolf3D engine graphics, it really doesn't feel like a Wolf3D engine game at all. People go on and on about Tom Hall and 'The Devs of Incredible Power' taking the Wolf3D engine to its absolute limit with Rise of the Triad, which always confused me. In my personal opinion, the two Blake Stone games are a much better example of 'taking the Wolf3D engine to its absolute limit'. Despite Rise of the Triad being an incredible game, it doesn't impress me with its use of the Wolf3D engine like Blake Stone does. Like I was saying, Blake Stone makes me feel legitimately surprised that it's nothing more than a Wolf3D engine game. Rise of the Triad doesn't give me that same shocked feeling. Blake Stone also feels far more polished and 'refined' than Rise of the Triad.
When it released, Blake Stone was actually the very peak and gold standard of '3D action games' (the name for the genre before 'Doom clone' and later 'first person shooter'). For one week. Only one week. Because Doom released one week after Blake Stone. And of course, as we all know, Doom stole the show. With it's slick, fancy, new game engine and graphics, Doom had the spotlight on it even before it released. So Blake Stone was overshadowed and largely forgotten about. Hell, I just discovered the franchise myself a few years ago back in 2018. And I'm glad I did. Really great games, as far as Wolf3D engine games go.
PS: Download and use the BStone sourceport. It's a much smoother experience with proper mouse and WASD keyboard controls, proper strafing controls, support for modern resolutions with much cleaner graphics, etc.

Blake Stone: Aliens of Gold was released about a year and a half after Wolfenstein 3D using the same engine. It takes full advantage of the engine and plays kinda like Wolfenstein 3D on crack, improved in every way. Unfortunately, this game was released exactly one week before Doom, so despite its quality it ended up being relatively obscure in comparison. 

If you like Wolfenstein, you will [i]love[/i] this. It's super fun, has a great style/aesthetic & overall feel, there's a ton of enemy variety, the soundtrack is funky, the palette & animations pop, level design is smart and diverse, weapon variety creates increasingly satisfying run & gun gameplay, and the game has aged gracefully (especially with the BStone source port). Unlike Wolfenstein, which grows increasingly tedious and labyrinthine as the game progresses, Blake Stone's levels are much more balanced. The first few missions are arguably the most complex and each mission has a bit of a different feel to separate it from the others. This results in the overall gameplay actually having a bit of a subtle but noticeable dramatic structure to it, which is pretty neat and not something I was expecting.

It's easy to tell that tons of love went into the making of this. The manual includes a comic book with the backstory (in addition to the Story option on the main menu). Every frame on every enemy looks fantastic. We can not only blow holes in some of our enemies but we can actually see through those holes as they die, which is extremely cool. The run & walk speeds feel better than Wolfenstein's. Enemy stagger feels less cheesy than in Wolfenstein; in Wolfenstein, you can permastagger any enemy with the machine gun but here you only get a momentary stagger occasionally so every enemy is as capable of dishing it out as we are. There's no firing through solid objects (opening/closing doors & around corners) like in Wolfenstein. We can backtrack to previous levels to find secrets we missed or to stock up on supplies. It launched with a a fantastic in-game automap function which Wolfenstein lacked. It's just a solid game if you're into this style of FPS and there is a [i]lot[/i] of gameplay to be had here with 66 fresh feeling levels to climb through. Also, the Plasma Discharge Unit, which handles like a rapid fire grenade launcher, feels incredible in this.

The few negatives are a bit nitpicky but worth mentioning. The game has an interesting scoring system that grades us on how much treasure we find, how many enemies we kill, and how many informants we keep alive. Scientists can be informants or enemy combatants and the only way to tell the difference is to pop a round off in the vicinity to see who attacks us or to talk to them (friendlies give supplies). This adds a lot of depth to the play, especially when we get scenarios with friendlies mixed with bad guys such that we can't just go in blasting or rely on splash damage, but there are a very few levels where this mechanic is a bit annoying due to informants blocking our path temporarily or standing close to explosives which we need to destroy to 100% the map. Only like 1% of the levels had them be a pain, however. Another minor annoyance is that some levels have Plasma Alien generators, that infinitely re-spawn these very dangerous but squishy energy alien thingies. The mechanic isn't explained anywhere, however, so in one of the early levels it's possible to waste a huge chunk of ammo before it's obvious they keep coming forever, since they're cockblocking the way into a room and we can't actually see them spawning. Once we know about the mechanic it's not that big a deal, however, and creates a solid "oh ♥♥♥♥" feeling whenever we see the Aliens, panicking to see if they're standalone or as part of a generator swarm, as the generators are only in a few maps.

I wish I had known about this when I was younger but it was still a blast with the source port. Worth it at full price if you're a fan of this type of FPS.
